entry.title: Homework 10 - Poisson Process Simulation
entry.content:
Introduction

While Homework 7 explored symmetric random walks with discrete steps (+1/-1), Homework 10 introduces a fundamentally different type of stochastic process: the counting process. Instead of tracking position in a bidirectional walk, we count the number of events (arrivals, occurrences) that happen over continuous time. This homework demonstrates how discretizing continuous time leads to one of the most important processes in probability theory: the Poisson process.

Problem Statement

Counting Process in Continuous Time

Consider a time interval [0, T] (e.g., T = 1 hour, 1 day, etc.) during which “events” or “successes” occur. These events:

  • Occur independently of each other
  • Are uniformly distributed in time (no preferred moments)
  • Happen at a constant average rate λ (events per unit time)

Goal: Simulate this process by:

  1. Dividing [0, T] into n small subintervals of width Δt = T/n
  2. In each subinterval, an event occurs with probability λ·Δt
  3. Counting the total number of events N(T) in the interval

Question: What stochastic process does this approximate? What are its theoretical properties?

Mathematical Formulation

Time discretization:

t₀ = 0, t₁ = Δt, t₂ = 2Δt, ..., tₙ = nΔt = T
where Δt = T/n

Event indicator in subinterval i:

Xᵢ ~ Bernoulli(p = λΔt)
Xᵢ = 1 with probability λΔt (event occurs)
Xᵢ = 0 with probability 1-λΔt (no event)

Total count at time T:

N(T) = X₁ + X₂ + ... + Xₙ = Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ Xᵢ

As n → ∞ (Δt → 0): This discrete approximation converges to a continuous-time counting process.

Theoretical Background

2.1 From Discrete to Continuous: The Limiting Process

Key Observation: As we take finer subdivisions (n → ∞), we have:

  • Each subinterval becomes infinitesimally small: Δt → 0
  • The probability of an event in any subinterval becomes tiny: λΔt → 0
  • But the expected number of events remains constant: E[N(T)] = nλΔt = λT

What does N(T) approximate?

Since N(T) = Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ Xᵢ where Xᵢ ~ Bernoulli(λΔt), we have:

N(T) ~ Binomial(n, p = λΔt = λT/n)

As n → ∞ with λT fixed, this binomial distribution converges to:

N(T) ~ Poisson(λT)

This is a Poisson process!

2.2 The Poisson Process: Definition and Properties

Definition (Poisson Process): A counting process {N(t), t ≥ 0} is a Poisson process with rate λ > 0 if:

  1. N(0) = 0 (starts at zero)

  2. Independent increments: For any times 0 ≤ t₁ < t₂ < t₃ < t₄: 
    N(t₂) - N(t₁) is independent of N(t₄) - N(t₃)

  3. Stationary increments: The distribution of N(t+s) - N(s) depends only on t, not on s

  4. Poisson distribution: For any t > 0: 
    N(t) ~ Poisson(λt)
P(N(t) = k) = e^(-λt) · (λt)^k / k!

Equivalent characterization (infinitesimal properties):

For small Δt > 0:

P(N(t+Δt) - N(t) = 1) = λΔt + o(Δt)
P(N(t+Δt) - N(t) = 0) = 1 - λΔt + o(Δt)
P(N(t+Δt) - N(t) ≥ 2) = o(Δt)

where o(Δt) represents terms that vanish faster than Δt as Δt → 0.

Interpretation: In a small time interval Δt:

  • Exactly one event occurs with probability ≈ λΔt
  • No events occur with probability ≈ 1 - λΔt
  • Multiple events are negligible (probability goes to zero faster)

2.3 Key Properties of the Poisson Process

Property 1: Distribution at time t

P(N(t) = k) = e^(-λt) · (λt)^k / k!

Property 2: Expected value

E[N(t)] = λt

Property 3: Variance

Var(N(t)) = λt

Property 4: Mean and variance are equal (characteristic of Poisson)

Property 5: Interarrival times

The time between consecutive events follows an exponential distribution:

T₁, T₂, T₃, ... ~ Exponential(λ)
f(t) = λe^(-λt), t ≥ 0
E[Tᵢ] = 1/λ

Property 6: Arrival times

The time of the k-th event follows a Gamma distribution:

Sₖ = T₁ + T₂ + ... + Tₖ ~ Gamma(k, λ)

Property 7: Memoryless property

Knowing that no event occurred until time s doesn’t change the distribution of waiting time for the next event.

Property 8: Superposition

If N₁(t) ~ PP(λ₁) and N₂(t) ~ PP(λ₂) are independent Poisson processes, then:

N(t) = N₁(t) + N₂(t) ~ PP(λ₁ + λ₂)

Property 9: Thinning

If events from PP(λ) are independently kept with probability p, the result is PP(pλ).

2.4 The Rate Parameter λ

Physical interpretation: λ is the average number of events per unit time.

Units:

  • If T is in hours and λ = 5, expect 5 events per hour
  • If T is in seconds and λ = 0.1, expect 0.1 events per second (1 event per 10 seconds)

Scaling:

  • In interval [0, t], expect λt events
  • Mean interarrival time is 1/λ

Examples:

  • λ = 10 customers/hour → Average of 10 customers per hour, 20 in 2 hours
  • λ = 0.5 failures/day → Average of 0.5 failures per day, 1 failure every 2 days
  • λ = 100 particles/second → Average of 100 particle detections per second

2.5 Connection to Random Walk (Homework 7)

Aspect Homework 7 (Random Walk) Homework 10 (Poisson Process)
Type Position process Counting process
Time Discrete steps Continuous time
State space {…, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, …} {0, 1, 2, 3, …}
Steps ±1 (bidirectional) +1 only (non-decreasing)
Distribution Transformed Binomial Poisson
Parameters p (step probability) λ (rate)
Path behavior Up/down fluctuations Monotone increasing jumps
Applications Price movements, signals Arrivals, failures, calls

Key difference: Random walk can go up or down; Poisson process only counts up (number of events is non-decreasing).

Methodology

3.1 Simulation Parameters

Fixed parameters:

  • T = 1: Time interval (normalized to [0,1])
  • n = 5000: Number of subintervals
  • Δt = T/n = 0.0002: Width of each subinterval

Variable parameters:

  • λ: Rate parameter (events per unit time)
    • Small rate: λ = 1 (expect 1 event in [0,1])
    • Medium rate: λ = 10 (expect 10 events)
    • Large rate: λ = 50 (expect 50 events)
  • n_simulations: Number of independent realizations (e.g., 1000)

3.2 Implementation Strategy

Step 1: Time discretization

Create time grid: t = [0, Δt, 2Δt, ..., T]

Step 2: Generate events

For each subinterval i:

Xᵢ ~ Bernoulli(λΔt)

This gives a sequence of 0s and 1s indicating when events occur.

Step 3: Cumulative counting

N(t) = cumulative sum of X₁, X₂, ..., Xₜ/Δₜ

This produces a step function: N(t) stays constant, then jumps by 1 when an event occurs.

Step 4: Multiple realizations

Repeat steps 2-3 many times to get distribution of:

  • N(T) (total count)
  • N(t) at various times t
  • Interarrival times

Step 5: Comparison with theory

  • Plot empirical distribution of N(T)
  • Overlay theoretical Poisson(λT) PMF
  • Calculate sample mean and variance
  • Compare with theoretical λT

3.3 Validation Checks

Check 1: Mean

E[N(T)] = λT
Sample mean should be close to λT

Check 2: Variance

Var(N(T)) = λT
Sample variance should be close to λT

Check 3: Distribution shape

Empirical histogram should match Poisson PMF

Check 4: Interarrival times

If we record times between events, they should follow Exponential(λ)

3.4 Visualization Strategy

Plot 1: Sample paths

  • Show several realizations of N(t) vs t
  • Display step function nature
  • Illustrate randomness in jump times

Plot 2: Distribution of N(T)

  • Histogram of final counts from many simulations
  • Overlay theoretical Poisson(λT) PMF
  • Include mean and variance annotations

Plot 3: Convergence analysis

  • Show how distribution changes with n (fineness of subdivision)
  • Demonstrate convergence to Poisson as n increases

Plot 4: Rate parameter effects

  • Compare processes with different λ values
  • Show how λ affects both count and variability

Plot 5: Interarrival times (optional)

  • Histogram of time differences between events
  • Overlay theoretical Exponential(λ) PDF

Python Implementation

View poisson_process.py

Expected Results and Analysis

4.1 Example 1: Low Rate (λ = 1)

Theoretical predictions:

  • E[N(1)] = 1
  • Var(N(1)) = 1
  • P(N(1) = 0) = e^(-1) ≈ 0.368
  • P(N(1) = 1) = e^(-1) ≈ 0.368
  • P(N(1) = 2) = e^(-1)/2 ≈ 0.184

Expected simulation results (n = 5000, 1000 realizations):

  • Sample mean of N(1): ≈ 1.00 ± 0.03
  • Sample variance: ≈ 1.00 ± 0.05
  • Proportion with 0 events: ≈ 37%
  • Proportion with 1 event: ≈ 37%
  • Proportion with 2 events: ≈ 18%

Sample paths:

  • Most paths will have 0, 1, or 2 jumps
  • Jumps occur at random times
  • Some paths stay at 0 (no events)

Figure 1: Sample paths of Poisson process with λ = 1. Most paths have 0-2 jumps over the interval [0,1].

Figure 2: Distribution of N(1) for λ = 1 showing excellent agreement with theoretical Poisson(1) PMF. Left: Histogram with PMF overlay. Right: Q-Q plot.

4.2 Example 2: Medium Rate (λ = 10)

Theoretical predictions:

  • E[N(1)] = 10
  • Var(N(1)) = 10
  • Standard deviation: √10 ≈ 3.16
  • Distribution becomes more symmetric (nearly bell-shaped)

Expected simulation results:

  • Sample mean: ≈ 10.0 ± 0.1
  • Sample variance: ≈ 10.0 ± 0.3
  • Range of N(1): typically 3 to 17 (approximately)
  • Shape: approximately normal by CLT

Sample paths:

  • Multiple jumps per realization
  • More continuous-looking due to frequent jumps
  • Clear increasing trend

Figure 3: Sample paths with λ = 10 showing multiple jumps and convergence to mean trajectory λt = 10t.

Figure 4: Distribution of N(1) for λ = 10. The distribution is approximately bell-shaped, consistent with Central Limit Theorem for large λ.

4.3 Example 3: High Rate (λ = 50)

Theoretical predictions:

  • E[N(1)] = 50
  • Var(N(1)] = 50
  • Standard deviation: √50 ≈ 7.07
  • Distribution very close to Normal(50, 50)

Expected simulation results:

  • Sample mean: ≈ 50.0 ± 0.2
  • Sample variance: ≈ 50.0 ± 1.0
  • Range of N(1): typically 35 to 65
  • Shape: nearly indistinguishable from normal

Sample paths:

  • Many jumps (approximately 50 per path)
  • Appears almost linear due to density of events
  • Small relative fluctuations

Figure 5: Sample paths with λ = 50. High event frequency makes paths appear nearly linear with small fluctuations around the mean.

Figure 6: Distribution of N(1) for λ = 50 is nearly normal, demonstrating convergence to Gaussian for large λ.

4.4 Convergence Analysis

Effect of n (number of subintervals):

n Δt = 1/n λΔt (for λ=10) Quality of approximation
10 0.1 1.0 Poor (λΔt too large)
100 0.01 0.1 Fair
1000 0.001 0.01 Good
5000 0.0002 0.002 Excellent
10000 0.0001 0.001 Excellent

Key requirement: λΔt « 1 (much less than 1)

Why? The Poisson approximation assumes:

  • At most one event per subinterval
  • If λΔt is large, multiple events become likely
  • Binomial(n, λ/n) → Poisson(λ) as n → ∞

Convergence demonstration:

As n increases from 10 to 10000:

  1. Distribution shape: Becomes smoother, matches Poisson PMF better
  2. Mean convergence: Sample mean → λT
  3. Variance convergence: Sample variance → λT
  4. PMF accuracy: P(N(T) = k) matches theory more closely

Figure 7: Convergence of discrete approximation to Poisson process. As n increases (finer subdivision), the empirical distribution converges to theoretical Poisson PMF. Note how λΔt becomes smaller, satisfying the requirement λΔt « 1.

Figure 8: Comparison of Poisson processes with different rates. Top: Sample paths showing increasing event frequency. Bottom: Distributions showing shift in mean and increase in variance with λ.

4.5 Statistical Validation

Chi-square goodness-of-fit test:

Compare empirical frequencies with theoretical Poisson probabilities:

χ² = Σₖ (Observed_k - Expected_k)² / Expected_k

For good fit: χ² should be small, p-value > 0.05

Kolmogorov-Smirnov test:

Compare empirical CDF with theoretical Poisson CDF:

D = max|F_empirical(k) - F_Poisson(k)|

For good fit: D should be small, p-value > 0.05

Mean and variance ratio:

For Poisson, mean = variance. Check:

Ratio = Sample Variance / Sample Mean ≈ 1

Values close to 1 support Poisson assumption.

4.6 Interarrival Time Analysis

Extracting interarrival times:

For each sample path, record times between consecutive events:

T₁ = time of 1st event
T₂ = time of 2nd event - time of 1st event
T₃ = time of 3rd event - time of 2nd event
...

Theoretical distribution:

Tᵢ ~ Exponential(λ)
f(t) = λe^(-λt)
E[T] = 1/λ

Validation:

  • Plot histogram of all interarrival times
  • Overlay exponential PDF
  • Check if sample mean ≈ 1/λ
  • Perform KS test for exponential fit

Example (λ = 10):

  • Expected mean interarrival: 1/10 = 0.1
  • Most interarrivals < 0.3
  • Exponential decay pattern

Figure 9: Interarrival time distribution for λ = 1. Left: Histogram with exponential PDF overlay. Right: Q-Q plot confirming exponential fit.

Figure 10: Interarrival time distribution for λ = 10 showing faster decay (shorter average waiting times between events).

Mathematical Derivations

5.1 Binomial → Poisson Convergence

Setup: Let N ~ Binomial(n, p) with np = λ (constant)

As n → ∞ and p → 0 with np = λ fixed:

P(N = k) = C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k)
         = [n!/(k!(n-k)!)] · (λ/n)^k · (1-λ/n)^(n-k)

Step 1: Simplify factorials

n!/(n-k)! = n(n-1)(n-2)...(n-k+1) → n^k as n → ∞

Step 2: Binomial coefficient

C(n,k)/n^k = n(n-1)...(n-k+1)/(k!·n^k) → 1/k! as n → ∞

Step 3: Exponential term

(1-λ/n)^n → e^(-λ) as n → ∞
(1-λ/n)^(-k) → 1 as n → ∞

Result:

P(N = k) → e^(-λ) · λ^k / k! = Poisson(λ) PMF

5.2 Properties from Infinitesimal Analysis

Setup: Divide [0,T] into n intervals of width Δt = T/n

Probability of event in one interval:

p = P(event in [t, t+Δt]) = λΔt + o(Δt)

Number of events in [0,T]:

N(T) ~ Binomial(n, p)
E[N(T)] = np = n · λT/n = λT
Var(N(T)) = np(1-p) ≈ np = λT (since p → 0)

Taking limit n → ∞:

N(T) → Poisson(λT)

5.3 Memoryless Property

Exponential distribution of interarrival times:

Given that no event has occurred until time s, the remaining wait time has the same distribution:

P(T > s+t | T > s) = P(T > t)

Proof:

P(T > s+t | T > s) = P(T > s+t) / P(T > s)
                    = e^(-λ(s+t)) / e^(-λs)
                    = e^(-λt)
                    = P(T > t)

This is why the Poisson process has “no memory” of past events.

Applications and Extensions

6.1 Real-World Applications

Telecommunications:

  • Phone calls arriving at a switchboard
  • Data packets arriving at a router
  • λ = average calls/packets per second

Queueing theory:

  • Customers arriving at a service center
  • Jobs submitted to a computer system
  • λ = arrival rate

Reliability engineering:

  • Equipment failures over time
  • Software bugs discovered during testing
  • λ = failure/bug discovery rate

Physics:

  • Radioactive decay (particle emissions)
  • Cosmic ray detections
  • λ = particle detection rate

Biology:

  • Mutations in DNA sequences
  • Neuron firings
  • λ = event rate per unit time/length

Finance:

  • Trading times in limit order books
  • Insurance claims arrival
  • λ = trades/claims per day

Conclusion

This homework has demonstrated that:

  1. Discretization of continuous time with infinitesimal event probabilities (λΔt) naturally leads to the Poisson process

  2. The Poisson process is characterized by:
    • Independent, stationary increments
    • Poisson-distributed counts: N(t) ~ Poisson(λt)
    • Exponentially-distributed interarrival times
    • Memoryless property

  3. The rate parameter λ represents the average number of events per unit time and completely characterizes the process

  4. Simulation convergence: As n increases (finer time subdivision), the discrete approximation converges to the true continuous-time Poisson process

  5. Theoretical validation: Simulated statistics (mean, variance, distribution shape) converge to theoretical predictions

  6. Practical applications: The Poisson process models countless real-world phenomena where events occur randomly over time

The transition from discrete Binomial random variables (Homework 7’s building block) to continuous-time counting reveals how fundamental probability concepts extend naturally from discrete to continuous domains.

References

  1. Ross, S. M. (2014). Introduction to Probability Models, 11th ed. Academic Press.
  2. Kingman, J. F. C. (1993). Poisson Processes. Oxford University Press.
  3. Çinlar, E. (2011). Probability and Stochastics. Springer.
  4. Karlin, S. & Taylor, H. M. (1975). A First Course in Stochastic Processes, 2nd ed. Academic Press.
  5. Grimmett, G. & Stirzaker, D. (2001). Probability and Random Processes, 3rd ed. Oxford University Press.

entry.title: Homework 9 - Probability Theory and Measure Theory
entry.content:
Introduction

This homework explores the foundational aspects of probability theory, examining how different interpretations of probability have evolved and how the axiomatic approach provides a unified mathematical framework. We will investigate the deep connection between probability theory and measure theory, and derive fundamental properties from the axioms of probability.

Part 1: Interpretations of Probability

1.1 Classical (Laplacian) Interpretation

Definition: The probability of an event A is the ratio of favorable outcomes to total possible outcomes, assuming all outcomes are equally likely.

P(A) = |A| / |Ω| = (Number of favorable outcomes) / (Total number of outcomes)

Example: Rolling a fair die, P(even number) = 3/6 = 0.5

Strengths:

  • Intuitive and easy to apply in simple cases
  • Provides exact calculations for finite, symmetric sample spaces
  • Foundation for combinatorial probability

Limitations:

  • Requires outcomes to be equally likely (circular reasoning)
  • Cannot handle continuous sample spaces
  • Fails for infinite sample spaces
  • Cannot address cases where symmetry is not obvious

Historical Context: Proposed by Pierre-Simon Laplace in the 18th century, this was the first systematic approach to probability.

1.2 Frequentist Interpretation

Definition: The probability of an event is the limiting relative frequency of its occurrence in an infinite sequence of independent trials.

P(A) = lim_{n→∞} (n_A / n)

where n_A is the number of times event A occurs in n trials.

Example: If we flip a coin 10,000 times and observe 5,023 heads, P(heads) ≈ 0.5023

Strengths:

  • Based on empirical observation
  • Applicable to real-world experiments
  • Provides operational meaning to probability
  • No need to assume equally likely outcomes

Limitations:

  • Requires repeatable experiments
  • Cannot handle one-time events (e.g., “probability of rain tomorrow”)
  • The limit may not exist in practice
  • Infinite repetition is physically impossible

Historical Context: Developed by Richard von Mises and others in the early 20th century as a response to the limitations of the classical approach.

1.3 Bayesian (Subjective) Interpretation

Definition: Probability represents a degree of belief or confidence about an event, updated through experience using Bayes’ theorem.

P(H|E) = P(E|H) · P(H) / P(E)

Key Concepts:

  • Prior probability P(H): Initial belief before observing evidence
  • Likelihood P(E|H): Probability of evidence given hypothesis
  • Posterior probability P(H|E): Updated belief after observing evidence

Example: Estimating the probability that a patient has a disease given test results

Strengths:

  • Handles one-time events and subjective uncertainties
  • Incorporates prior knowledge
  • Natural framework for updating beliefs with new information
  • Applicable to decision-making under uncertainty

Limitations:

  • Different individuals may assign different prior probabilities
  • Subjective nature can lead to disagreements
  • Choice of prior can significantly influence results
  • Requires careful elicitation of beliefs

Betting Mechanism: To quantify subjective probability, consider: “How much would you be willing to bet to receive $100 if event A occurs?” If you’d bet $p, then your subjective probability is P(A) = p/100. Additionally, you should be willing to take either side of the bet at these odds.

Historical Context: Foundations laid by Thomas Bayes (18th century), developed extensively by Bruno de Finetti and Leonard Savage in the 20th century.

1.4 Geometric (Continuous) Interpretation

Definition: For continuous sample spaces, probability is determined by geometric measures (length, area, volume).

P(A) = measure(A) / measure(Ω)

Example: Probability that a randomly chosen point in a unit square falls in a specific region

Strengths:

  • Extends probability to continuous spaces
  • Natural for physical problems (e.g., particle positions)
  • Foundation for continuous random variables

Limitations:

  • Requires careful definition of “random” selection
  • Some sets may not be measurable (Vitali set)
  • Paradoxes can arise (Bertrand’s paradox)

1.5 Conceptual Inconsistencies Resolved by Axiomatic Approach

Problems Among Interpretations:

  1. Circular reasoning in classical approach: Defining probability using “equally likely” outcomes assumes what we’re trying to define

  2. Incompatibility: Frequentist approach cannot handle unique events; Bayesian allows them but is subjective

  3. Infinite sample spaces: Classical approach breaks down; geometric approach introduces measurability issues

  4. Mathematical rigor: None of the interpretations provides a rigorous mathematical foundation

Resolution through Axioms:

The axiomatic approach, proposed by Andrei Kolmogorov (1933), provides a unified mathematical framework independent of interpretation:

Kolmogorov’s Axioms:

  1. Non-negativity: P(A) ≥ 0 for all events A
  2. Normalization: P(Ω) = 1 (certainty of sample space)
  3. Countable additivity: For disjoint events A₁, A₂, …: 
    P(⋃ᵢ Aᵢ) = Σᵢ P(Aᵢ)

Why This Resolves Inconsistencies:

  • Interpretation-independent: The axioms don’t specify what probability means, only how it must behave mathematically
  • Mathematical rigor: Built on measure theory, a solid mathematical foundation
  • Universality: All interpretations must satisfy these axioms
  • Consistency: Different interpretations can coexist as different ways to assign probabilities, but all must obey the same rules

Example: Both a frequentist (using relative frequencies) and a Bayesian (using degrees of belief) can work with the same probability space (Ω, F, P) as long as their probability assignments satisfy the axioms.

Part 2: Probability Theory and Measure Theory

2.1 Measure Theory Foundation

Measure Space: A triplet (Ω, F, μ) where:

  • Ω: Set of all elements (universal set)
  • F: σ-algebra on Ω (collection of measurable sets)
  • μ: Measure function, μ: F → [0, ∞]

Properties of a Measure:

  1. Non-negativity: μ(A) ≥ 0 for all A ∈ F
  2. Null empty set: μ(∅) = 0
  3. Countable additivity: For disjoint sets A₁, A₂, …: 
    μ(⋃ᵢ Aᵢ) = Σᵢ μ(Aᵢ)

2.2 σ-Algebras (Sigma-Algebras)

Definition: A σ-algebra F on a set Ω is a collection of subsets satisfying:

  1. Contains Ω: Ω ∈ F
  2. Closed under complementation: If A ∈ F, then Aᶜ ∈ F
  3. Closed under countable unions: If A₁, A₂, … ∈ F, then ⋃ᵢ Aᵢ ∈ F

Consequences:

  • ∅ ∈ F (since ∅ = Ωᶜ)
  • Closed under countable intersections (by De Morgan’s laws)
  • Closed under set differences

Why σ-Algebras?

σ-algebras define which subsets are “measurable” (i.e., which events can be assigned probabilities). Not all subsets can be measurable without leading to contradictions (e.g., Vitali sets in ℝ).

Example: For Ω = {1, 2, 3}, one possible σ-algebra is:

F = {∅, {1}, {2,3}, {1,2,3}}

Common σ-Algebras:

  • Power set: F = P(Ω), all subsets (for finite/countable Ω)
  • Borel σ-algebra: Generated by open sets in ℝⁿ (for continuous spaces)
  • Trivial σ-algebra: F = {∅, Ω}

2.3 Probability Measures

Definition: A probability measure P is a measure on (Ω, F) such that:

P(Ω) = 1

Thus, a probability space is a measure space (Ω, F, P) where:

  • Ω: Sample space (all possible outcomes)
  • F: Event space (all events we can assign probabilities to)
  • P: Probability measure (assigns probabilities to events)

2.4 Measurable Functions and Random Variables

Measurable Function: A function f: (Ω, F) → (S, Σ) is measurable if:

f⁻¹(B) ∈ F  for all B ∈ Σ

i.e., the preimage of every measurable set in S is measurable in Ω.

Random Variable: A measurable function X: (Ω, F, P) → (ℝ, B, P_X) where:

  • Ω: Sample space
  • F: σ-algebra of events
  • P: Probability measure on (Ω, F)
  • B: Borel σ-algebra on ℝ
  • P_X: Induced probability measure on ℝ (distribution of X)

Why This Definition?

For X to be a random variable, we need to be able to calculate probabilities like P(X ∈ B) for any Borel set B. This requires:

{ω ∈ Ω : X(ω) ∈ B} ∈ F

i.e., X⁻¹(B) must be an event in our probability space.

Example from Random Walk:

In Homework 7, each step Xᵢ is a random variable:

Xᵢ: Ω → {-1, +1}

where Ω represents all possible outcomes of week i (secure or breached), and:

  • Xᵢ⁻¹({+1}) = {server secure} ∈ F
  • Xᵢ⁻¹({-1}) = {server breached} ∈ F

The cumulative score S(n) = X₁ + X₂ + … + Xₙ is also a random variable.

2.5 Summary of Connections

Measure Theory Probability Theory
Measure space (Ω, F, μ) Probability space (Ω, F, P)
Measure μ Probability measure P
μ(Ω) ∈ [0, ∞] P(Ω) = 1
Measurable set A ∈ F Event A
Measurable function Random variable
μ(A) P(A)

Key Insight: Probability theory is measure theory with the additional constraint that the total measure equals 1. This connection provides probability theory with rigorous mathematical foundations.

Part 3: Deriving Properties from Axioms

3.1 Basic Properties

From Kolmogorov’s axioms, we can derive:

Property 1: Probability of Empty Set

P(∅) = 0

Proof: Let A₁ = Ω and Aᵢ = ∅ for i > 1. These are disjoint, so:

P(Ω) = P(⋃ᵢ Aᵢ) = P(Ω) + P(∅) + P(∅) + ...
1 = 1 + Σᵢ₌₂^∞ P(∅)

This is only possible if P(∅) = 0. □

Property 2: Complement Rule

P(Aᶜ) = 1 - P(A)

Proof: Since A and Aᶜ are disjoint and A ∪ Aᶜ = Ω:

P(Ω) = P(A ∪ Aᶜ) = P(A) + P(Aᶜ)
1 = P(A) + P(Aᶜ)
P(Aᶜ) = 1 - P(A)

□

Property 3: Monotonicity

If A ⊆ B, then P(A) ≤ P(B)

Proof: We can write B = A ∪ (B ∩ Aᶜ), where A and (B ∩ Aᶜ) are disjoint:

P(B) = P(A) + P(B ∩ Aᶜ)

Since P(B ∩ Aᶜ) ≥ 0 (non-negativity axiom):

P(B) ≥ P(A)

□

3.2 Subadditivity Property

Theorem (Subadditivity): For any sequence of events A₁, A₂, A₃, … (not necessarily disjoint):

P(⋃ᵢ₌₁^∞ Aᵢ) ≤ Σᵢ₌₁^∞ P(Aᵢ)

For finite case (n events):

P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ ... ∪ Aₙ) ≤ P(A₁) + P(A₂) + ... + P(Aₙ)

Proof (Countable Case):

Define a sequence of disjoint events:

B₁ = A₁
B₂ = A₂ ∩ A₁ᶜ
B₃ = A₃ ∩ A₁ᶜ ∩ A₂ᶜ
...
Bₙ = Aₙ ∩ (⋃ᵢ₌₁^(n-1) Aᵢ)ᶜ

These events are disjoint by construction, and:

⋃ᵢ₌₁^∞ Bᵢ = ⋃ᵢ₌₁^∞ Aᵢ

By countable additivity:

P(⋃ᵢ₌₁^∞ Aᵢ) = P(⋃ᵢ₌₁^∞ Bᵢ) = Σᵢ₌₁^∞ P(Bᵢ)

Since Bᵢ ⊆ Aᵢ for all i, by monotonicity P(Bᵢ) ≤ P(Aᵢ):

P(⋃ᵢ₌₁^∞ Aᵢ) = Σᵢ₌₁^∞ P(Bᵢ) ≤ Σᵢ₌₁^∞ P(Aᵢ)

□

Interpretation: The probability of a union is at most the sum of individual probabilities. Equality holds only when events are disjoint (no overlap).

Example: In security analysis, if event Aᵢ represents “breach occurs through vulnerability i”, then:

P(at least one breach) ≤ P(breach through vuln. 1) + ... + P(breach through vuln. n)

This is often called the union bound or Boole’s inequality.

3.3 Inclusion-Exclusion Principle

Theorem (Inclusion-Exclusion): For any events A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ:

P(⋃ᵢ₌₁ⁿ Aᵢ) = Σᵢ P(Aᵢ) - Σᵢ<ⱼ P(Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ) + Σᵢ<ⱼ<ₖ P(Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ ∩ Aₖ) - ... + (-1)ⁿ⁺¹ P(A₁ ∩ ... ∩ Aₙ)

Proof by Induction:

Base case (n=2):

P(A₁ ∪ A₂) = P(A₁) + P(A₂) - P(A₁ ∩ A₂)

Proof: Write A₁ ∪ A₂ as disjoint union:

A₁ ∪ A₂ = A₁ ∪ (A₂ ∩ A₁ᶜ)

Then:

P(A₁ ∪ A₂) = P(A₁) + P(A₂ ∩ A₁ᶜ)

Also, A₂ = (A₂ ∩ A₁) ∪ (A₂ ∩ A₁ᶜ), so:

P(A₂) = P(A₂ ∩ A₁) + P(A₂ ∩ A₁ᶜ)
P(A₂ ∩ A₁ᶜ) = P(A₂) - P(A₁ ∩ A₂)

Substituting:

P(A₁ ∪ A₂) = P(A₁) + P(A₂) - P(A₁ ∩ A₂)

□

Inductive step: Assume the formula holds for n events. For n+1 events:

Let B = ⋃ᵢ₌₁ⁿ Aᵢ. Then:

P(⋃ᵢ₌₁ⁿ⁺¹ Aᵢ) = P(B ∪ Aₙ₊₁) = P(B) + P(Aₙ₊₁) - P(B ∩ Aₙ₊₁)

By inductive hypothesis, P(B) satisfies inclusion-exclusion. Also:

B ∩ Aₙ₊₁ = ⋃ᵢ₌₁ⁿ (Aᵢ ∩ Aₙ₊₁)

Applying inclusion-exclusion to this union and substituting gives the formula for n+1 events. □

Alternative Proof (Combinatorial):

Each element ω ∈ ⋃ᵢ Aᵢ belongs to exactly k ≥ 1 of the sets A₁, …, Aₙ.

On the right-hand side, this element is counted:

  • In Σᵢ P(Aᵢ): k times
  • In -Σᵢ<ⱼ P(Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ): -C(k,2) times
  • In Σᵢ<ⱼ<ₖ P(Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ ∩ Aₖ): +C(k,3) times
  • etc.

Total count:

C(k,1) - C(k,2) + C(k,3) - ... + (-1)ᵏ⁺¹C(k,k) = 1 - (1-1)ᵏ = 1

(by binomial theorem), which matches the left-hand side. □

Special Cases:

For n=3:

P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ A₃) = P(A₁) + P(A₂) + P(A₃) 
                   - P(A₁ ∩ A₂) - P(A₁ ∩ A₃) - P(A₂ ∩ A₃)
                   + P(A₁ ∩ A₂ ∩ A₃)

Comparison with Subadditivity:

Inclusion-exclusion gives an exact formula, while subadditivity gives an upper bound:

P(⋃ᵢ Aᵢ) = Σᵢ P(Aᵢ) - [correction terms] ≤ Σᵢ P(Aᵢ)

The correction terms account for overlaps (double-counting).

3.4 Applications and Examples

Example 1: Security Systems

A server has three independent vulnerabilities with exploit probabilities:

  • P(A₁) = 0.3
  • P(A₂) = 0.2
  • P(A₃) = 0.4

What is P(at least one vulnerability exploited)?

Subadditivity bound:

P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ A₃) ≤ 0.3 + 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.9

If independent (P(Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ) = P(Aᵢ)P(Aⱼ)):

P(A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ A₃) = 0.3 + 0.2 + 0.4 
                  - 0.06 - 0.12 - 0.08 
                  + 0.024
                  = 0.664

Or equivalently:

P(no exploit) = (1-0.3)(1-0.2)(1-0.4) = 0.336
P(at least one) = 1 - 0.336 = 0.664

Example 2: Counting Principles

How many integers from 1 to 100 are divisible by 2, 3, or 5?

Let:

  • A₁ = {divisible by 2}
  • A₂ = {divisible by 3}
  • A₃ = {divisible by 5}

Then:

|A₁| = 50, |A₂| = 33, |A₃| = 20
|A₁ ∩ A₂| = 16, |A₁ ∩ A₃| = 10, |A₂ ∩ A₃| = 6
|A₁ ∩ A₂ ∩ A₃| = 3

By inclusion-exclusion:

|A₁ ∪ A₂ ∪ A₃| = 50 + 33 + 20 - 16 - 10 - 6 + 3 = 74

3.5 Generalization: Bonferroni Inequalities

The inclusion-exclusion principle leads to alternating upper and lower bounds:

Lower bounds (odd k):

P(⋃ᵢ Aᵢ) ≥ S₁ - S₂ + S₃ - ... + S₂ₖ₋₁

Upper bounds (even k):

P(⋃ᵢ Aᵢ) ≤ S₁ - S₂ + S₃ - ... - S₂ₖ

where Sₖ is the sum of probabilities of all k-way intersections:

S₁ = Σᵢ P(Aᵢ)
S₂ = Σᵢ<ⱼ P(Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ)
S₃ = Σᵢ<ⱼ<ₖ P(Aᵢ ∩ Aⱼ ∩ Aₖ)
...

Conclusion

This homework has demonstrated:

  1. Multiple interpretations of probability exist (classical, frequentist, Bayesian, geometric), each with strengths and limitations

  2. The axiomatic approach provides a unified mathematical framework that resolves conceptual inconsistencies by defining probability as a normalized measure

  3. Measure theory provides the rigorous foundation for probability theory through:
    • σ-algebras (defining measurable events)
    • Probability measures (assigning probabilities)
    • Measurable functions (random variables)

  4. Fundamental properties like subadditivity and inclusion-exclusion can be rigorously derived from Kolmogorov’s axioms

  5. Practical applications of these principles appear throughout statistics, from security analysis to combinatorial counting

The connection between probability and measure theory, established by Kolmogorov, transformed probability from a collection of intuitions into a rigorous mathematical discipline.

References

  1. Kolmogorov, A. N. (1933). Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung. Springer. (English: Foundations of the Theory of Probability, 1950)
  2. Billingsley, P. (1995). Probability and Measure, 3rd ed. Wiley.
  3. Feller, W. (1968). An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1, 3rd ed. Wiley.
  4. Ross, S. M. (2014). A First Course in Probability, 9th ed. Pearson.
  5. Durrett, R. (2019). Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed. Cambridge University Press.

entry.title: Homework 8 - Comparing Bernoulli and Random Walk Processes
entry.content:
Introduction: Two Perspectives on Binary Random Processes

Homework 4 and Homework 7 explored two fundamental ways to model sequences of binary random outcomes. While both involve independent trials with two possible results, they differ profoundly in their mathematical structure, interpretation, and applications. This homework provides a comprehensive comparison, highlighting the deep connections between these seemingly different processes.

Core Question: What changes when we shift from counting successes (Homework 4) to tracking signed displacements (Homework 7)?

Side-by-Side Comparison

Basic Setup

Aspect Homework 4: Bernoulli Process Homework 7: Random Walk
Process Name Law of Large Numbers Simulation Symmetric/Asymmetric Random Walk
Trial Outcome Success (1) or Failure (0) Step Up (+1) or Step Down (-1)
Cumulative Quantity Number of successes: k Net displacement: s = 2k - n
Range After n Trials k ∈ {0, 1, 2, …, n} s ∈ {-n, -n+2, …, n-2, n}
Possible Values n + 1 values n + 1 values (same parity as n)
Starting Point k = 0 s = 0
Direction Monotone increasing (k ≥ 0) Bidirectional (s can be negative)

Mathematical Formulation

Homework 4 (Bernoulli Process):

Xᵢ ∈ {0, 1}
K(n) = Σ Xᵢ  (total successes)
E[K(n)] = np
Var[K(n)] = np(1-p)

Homework 7 (Random Walk):

Yᵢ ∈ {-1, +1}
S(n) = Σ Yᵢ  (net displacement)
E[S(n)] = n(q-p') = n(2q-1)
Var[S(n)] = 4nqp'

where q = P(Yᵢ = +1) and p’ = P(Yᵢ = -1) = 1-q.

The Fundamental Transformation

The two processes are related by a simple transformation:

S(n) = 2K(n) - n
K(n) = (n + S(n)) / 2

Example: After n=10 trials with k=7 successes:

  • Homework 4: Position k = 7
  • Homework 7: Score s = 2(7) - 10 = 4

This transformation:

  • Maps [0, n] → [-n, n]
  • Stretches the range by factor of 2
  • Centers around 0 instead of n/2
  • Preserves the combinatorial structure

Visualization Differences

Homework 4 Trajectories:

f(t) = K(t) / t  (relative frequency)
  • Trajectories start at variable points (0 or 1)
  • Converge toward horizontal line at p
  • Always bounded: 0 ≤ f(t) ≤ 1
  • Focus: convergence behavior

Homework 7 Trajectories:

S(t) = 2K(t) - t  (cumulative score)
  • All trajectories start at 0
  • Can wander above and below starting point
  • Unbounded: -t ≤ S(t) ≤ t
  • Focus: path structure and excursions

Mathematical Connections

1. Binomial Coefficients: The Unifying Structure

Both processes use the same counting mechanism:

Number of paths reaching position k (HW4) or score s (HW7):

N(n, k) = C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n-k)!)

For Homework 7, score s corresponds to k = (n+s)/2 successes:

N(n, s) = C(n, (n+s)/2)

Example (n=6):

k (HW4) s (HW7) Paths C(6,k)
0 -6 1
1 -4 6
2 -2 15
3 0 20
4 +2 15
5 +4 6
6 +6 1

Observation: Same combinatorial structure, different interpretation:

  • HW4: “How many ways to choose k successes from 6 trials?”
  • HW7: “How many paths reach score s after 6 steps?”

2. Pascal’s Triangle: The Universal Structure

Both homeworks generate Pascal’s triangle, but read it differently:

Pascal’s Triangle (n=0 to n=6):

                    1
                  1   1
                1   2   1
              1   3   3   1
            1   4   6   4   1
          1   5  10  10   5   1
        1   6  15  20  15   6   1

Homework 4 Reading (row n=6):

  • Position k: Number of ways to get exactly k successes in 6 trials
  • Values: {1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1} for k ∈ {0,1,2,3,4,5,6}

Homework 7 Reading (row n=6):

  • Position s: Number of paths reaching score s after 6 steps
  • Values: {1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1} for s ∈ {-6,-4,-2,0,2,4,6}

The mapping: Same numbers, stretched coordinate system (s = 2k - n).

3. Recurrence Relations

Both satisfy the same fundamental recurrence:

Combinatorial Form:

C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k)

Homework 4 Interpretation: “To have k successes in n trials, either:

  • Last trial was success, and we had k-1 successes in first n-1 trials, OR
  • Last trial was failure, and we had k successes in first n-1 trials”

Homework 7 Interpretation:

N(n, s) = N(n-1, s-1) + N(n-1, s+1)

“To reach position s at step n, we must have been at:

  • Position s-1 at step n-1 and moved up (+1), OR
  • Position s+1 at step n-1 and moved down (-1)”

Graphical representation:

            Step n-1      Step n
           •  (s+1)
            \
             \  (-1)
              ↘
               •           (s)
              ↗
             /  (+1)
            /
           •  (s-1)

4. Binomial Distribution Connection

Homework 4: Direct binomial distribution

P(K = k) = C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k)

Homework 7: Transformed binomial distribution

P(S = s) = P(K = (n+s)/2) = C(n, (n+s)/2) q^((n+s)/2) p'^((n-s)/2)

where:

  • K = number of +1 steps (successes)
  • S = 2K - n (net displacement)
  • k = (n+s)/2 relates the two

Distribution shape:

  • Both are binomial distributions
  • HW7 is HW4 stretched and centered at 0
  • Same bell curve, different x-axis scale

5. Binomial Expansion

The binomial theorem provides the foundation for both:

(A + B)^n = Σ(k=0 to n) C(n,k) A^k B^(n-k)

Setting A = B = 1:

2^n = Σ C(n,k)

Interpretation:

  • Total trajectories: 2^n (each of n steps has 2 choices)
  • Sum of all path counts: Σ C(n,k) = 2^n ✓

Homework 4: 2^n total sequences of n binary outcomes Homework 7: 2^n total random walk paths through n steps

Example (n=5):

2^5 = 32 = C(5,0) + C(5,1) + C(5,2) + C(5,3) + C(5,4) + C(5,5)
        = 1 + 5 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1

6. Fibonacci Sequence Connection

Hidden within Pascal’s triangle are the Fibonacci numbers, obtained by summing diagonals:

                    1
                  1   1
                1   2   1
              1   3   3   1
            1   4   6   4   1
          1   5  10  10   5   1
        1   6  15  20  15   6   1

Diagonal sums:
F(1) = 1
F(2) = 1 + 1 = 1
F(3) = 1 + 2 = 2
F(4) = 1 + 3 + 1 = 3
F(5) = 1 + 4 + 3 = 5
F(6) = 1 + 5 + 6 + 1 = 8
F(7) = 1 + 6 + 10 + 4 = 13

Formula:

F(n) = Σ(k=0 to ⌊n/2⌋) C(n-k-1, k)

Connection to our homeworks:

  • Fibonacci appears when counting paths with constraints
  • Example: Number of ways to reach position n using steps of size 1 or 2
  • Related to lattice paths, which generalize both HW4 and HW7 structures

7. Symmetry Properties

Homework 4 (p = 0.5):

P(K = k) = P(K = n-k)
C(n,k) = C(n, n-k)

Distribution is symmetric around k = n/2.

Homework 7 (q = p’ = 0.5):

P(S = s) = P(S = -s)
N(n,s) = N(n,-s)

Distribution is symmetric around s = 0.

Asymmetry: When p ≠ 0.5 (HW4) or q ≠ p’ (HW7):

  • HW4: Distribution skews toward larger k if p > 0.5
  • HW7: Random walk drifts positive if q > p’, negative if q < p’

Key Differences

1. Conceptual Framework

Aspect Homework 4 Homework 7
Central Question “What proportion of trials succeed?” “Where do we end up?”
Accumulation One-directional (counting up) Bidirectional (up and down)
Focus Convergence to probability Path behavior and position
Key Theorem Law of Large Numbers Random Walk Theory
Application Frequency estimation Position tracking

2. Range and Scale

Homework 4:

  • Range: [0, n]
  • n+1 possible values
  • Relative frequency: f(n) = k/n ∈ [0, 1]

Homework 7:

  • Range: [-n, n]
  • n+1 possible values (same parity)
  • Score: s ∈ {-n, -n+2, …, n-2, n}

Scale transformation: s = 2k - n maps HW4 → HW7

3. Visualization Differences

Homework 4 plots:

f(n) vs n (relative frequency over trials)
- Trajectories converge to horizontal line at p
- Y-axis: [0, 1]
- Shows LLN convergence behavior

Homework 7 plots:

S(n) vs n (cumulative score over steps)
- Trajectories start at origin, wander up/down
- Y-axis: [-n, n]
- Shows random walk structure

4. Statistical Interpretation

Homework 4:

Mean: E[K] = np
Variance: Var[K] = np(1-p)
Distribution: K ~ Binomial(n, p)

Homework 7:

Mean: E[S] = n(q-p') = n(2q-1)
Variance: Var[S] = 4nqp'
Distribution: S ~ 2·Binomial(n, q) - n

Expected position:

  • HW4: Expected successes = np
  • HW7: Expected score = n(q-p’)
    • If q = p’ = 0.5: E[S] = 0 (symmetric walk)
    • If q > p’: E[S] > 0 (positive drift)
    • If q < p’: E[S] < 0 (negative drift)

5. Probability Calculations

Homework 4: P(exactly k successes)

P(K = k) = C(n,k) p^k (1-p)^(n-k)

Homework 7: P(final score = s)

P(S = s) = C(n, (n+s)/2) q^((n+s)/2) p'^((n-s)/2)

Example (n=10, p=0.6 → q=0.6, p’=0.4):

k (HW4) P(K=k) s (HW7) P(S=s)
0 0.0001 -10 0.0001
5 0.2007 0 0.2007
8 0.1209 +6 0.1209
10 0.0060 +10 0.0060

Same probabilities, different coordinate systems!

Practical Applications

Homework 4 Applications: Success Rate Estimation

  1. Quality Control:
    • n = sample size
    • k = number of defective items
    • Estimate defect rate: p̂ = k/n
  2. A/B Testing:
    • n = number of users
    • k = number of conversions
    • Estimate conversion rate
  3. Medical Trials:
    • n = patients
    • k = successful treatments
    • Estimate treatment efficacy

Key insight: LLN guarantees that k/n → p as n increases.

Homework 7 Applications: Position Tracking

  1. Financial Markets:
    • S(n) = cumulative price changes
    • Predict drift (bull vs bear market)
    • Analyze volatility
  2. Game Theory:
    • S(n) = player’s score relative to opponent
    • Winning = reaching positive threshold
    • “Gambler’s ruin” problems
  3. Physical Systems:
    • Brownian motion (continuous limit of random walk)
    • Particle diffusion
    • Stock price modeling
  4. Network Security (our problem):
    • S(n) = net security score
    • Positive = more secure weeks than breached
    • Negative = system under heavy attack

Key insight: Random walks model cumulative effects of balanced forces.

Convergence Behavior

Homework 4: Convergence to Probability

Law of Large Numbers:

f(n) = K/n → p  as n → ∞

Rate of convergence:

Var[f(n)] = p(1-p)/n → 0  as n → ∞

Central Limit Theorem:

√n (f(n) - p) → N(0, p(1-p))

Practical meaning:

  • With 1000 trials, f(1000) ≈ p ± 0.03 (roughly)
  • Uncertainty decreases as 1/√n

Homework 7: Spreading Distribution

Expected position:

E[S(n)] = n(q - p')

Standard deviation:

σ[S(n)] = 2√(nqp')

Central Limit Theorem:

(S(n) - n(q-p')) / (2√(nqp')) → N(0, 1)

Practical meaning:

  • Position spreads as √n
  • Even with drift, substantial randomness remains
  • After 1000 steps: typical deviation ≈ 30 steps from expected position

Combined Visualization

To see the relationship, we can plot both perspectives simultaneously:

Example: n=100, p=0.6 (or q=0.6, p’=0.4)

View bernoulli_rand_walk_comp.py

Figure 1: Side-by-side comparison of the same binary process viewed as Bernoulli trials (left) and random walk (right). Both use n=100, p=0.6, showing 50 trajectories. Left panel shows relative frequencies converging to p=0.6, while right panel shows cumulative scores drifting toward expected value of 20.

Deep Mathematical Connections

1. Generating Functions

Binomial coefficients generating function:

(1 + x)^n = Σ(k=0 to n) C(n,k) x^k

Applications:

  • Extract C(n,k) as coefficient of x^k
  • Proves identities like Σ C(n,k) = 2^n (set x=1)
  • Connects to probability generating functions

2. Catalan Numbers

Related to Pascal’s triangle via:

Cat(n) = C(2n, n) / (n+1)

Connection to random walks:

  • Catalan numbers count paths that never go below starting point
  • “Ballot problem”: paths where cumulative score stays ≥ 0
  • Appears in HW7 when adding boundary constraints

3. Stirling’s Approximation

For large n:

C(n, n/2) ≈ 2^n / √(πn/2)

Implications:

  • Central binomial coefficient (most probable outcome)
  • Both HW4 and HW7 peak probabilities
  • Explains bell curve shape in histograms

4. Reflection Principle

Random walk theorem: Number of paths from (0,0) to (n,k) that touch or cross y=-1:

= Number of paths from (0,-2) to (n,k)

Application: Calculate probability of first return to origin, hitting boundaries, etc.

Summary Table

Property Homework 4 Homework 7
Process Type Bernoulli trials Random walk
Outcome Space {0, 1} {-1, +1}
Cumulative Variable K ∈ [0, n] S ∈ [-n, n]
Path Count C(n,k) C(n, (n+s)/2)
Total Paths 2^n 2^n
Distribution Binomial(n,p) Transformed Binomial
Expected Value np n(q-p’)
Variance np(1-p) 4nqp’
Convergence f(n)→p S(n)/n→(q-p’)
Spread O(√n) absolute O(√n) absolute
Relative Spread O(1/√n) O(1/√n) relative to position
Key Theorem LLN + CLT Random Walk CLT
Symmetry Axis k = n/2 s = 0
Pascal’s Triangle Direct reading Stretched reading
Focus Rate/proportion Position/displacement

Conclusion

Homeworks 4 and 7 explore the same fundamental combinatorial structure—the binomial distribution—from two complementary perspectives:

Homework 4 (Bernoulli Process):

  • Counts successes: “How many heads?”
  • Converges to probability via LLN
  • Application: Estimating rates and proportions
  • Range: [0, n], monotone increasing

Homework 7 (Random Walk):

  • Tracks net displacement: “How far up or down?”
  • Wanders around expected drift
  • Application: Position tracking, cumulative effects
  • Range: [-n, n], bidirectional movement

Unified Mathematics: Both homeworks use:

  1. Binomial coefficients C(n,k) for path counting
  2. Pascal’s triangle for recursive structure
  3. Binomial distribution for probability calculations
  4. 2^n total trajectories from binary choices
  5. Central Limit Theorem for asymptotic behavior

Key Transformation:

S(n) = 2K(n) - n

This simple linear mapping connects the two perspectives while preserving the underlying combinatorial structure.

Deeper Insight: The random walk (HW7) is not just a different view of Bernoulli trials (HW4)—it’s a fundamental model in its own right, with applications ranging from finance to physics to computer science. The connection through binomial coefficients reveals the deep unity in probability theory: different phenomena share common mathematical structures.

Educational Value: By studying both perspectives, we gain:

  • Combinatorial intuition: Same counts, different interpretations
  • Probabilistic thinking: From frequencies to displacements
  • Mathematical connections: Pascal, Fibonacci, binomial theorem
  • Applied modeling: When to use each framework

The beauty of mathematics lies in these connections—seemingly different problems revealing identical structures underneath.

References

  1. Feller, W. (1968). An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1, 3rd ed. Wiley.
    • Chapters 3 (Bernoulli trials) and 14 (Random walks)
  2. Lawler, G. F. (2006). Introduction to Stochastic Processes, 2nd ed. Chapman & Hall.
    • Comprehensive treatment of random walks
  3. Ross, S. M. (1996). Stochastic Processes, 2nd ed. Wiley.
    • Connections between different stochastic models
  4. Graham, R. L., Knuth, D. E., & Patashnik, O. (1994). Concrete Mathematics, 2nd ed. Addison-Wesley.
    • Binomial coefficients, generating functions, and combinatorial identities
  5. Grimmett, G. & Stirzaker, D. (2001). Probability and Random Processes, 3rd ed. Oxford University Press.
    • Rigorous treatment of convergence theorems
